sections.title_en: The Mitzvot Dependent on the Land in General
sections.body_en:
The Torah was given to Israel so that they would study it and fulfil its mitzvot in the Land of Israel, and through this blessing would be drawn to the Land and from it to the whole world. For in the Land of Israel the kingship of God, His Torah and His blessing are revealed, and from it they spread to the whole world, whereas outside the Land it is difficult to reveal them. Therefore in the Land it is revealed that the Lord is God, whereas outside the Land He is called only "God of gods." Therefore the Sages said that a Jew who lives outside the Land is like one who worships idols (Ketubot 110b). They also said: "As long as you are in the Land, I am your God; when you are not in the Land, it is as if I am not your God" (Tosefta Avoda Zara 4:5). Therefore they said that the mitzva of settling the Land is equivalent to all the mitzvot (Sifrei Re'eh 80; Ramban, Vayikra 18:25).

It is also stated: "For you are crossing the Jordan to come and possess the land that the Lord your God is giving you, and you shall possess it and dwell in it. And you shall be careful to do all the statutes and the ordinances that I set before you this day. These are the statutes and the ordinances that you shall be careful to do in the land that the Lord, the God of your fathers, has given you to possess, all the days that you live upon the earth" (Devarim 11:32-12:1). This implies that the obligation of the mitzvot applies specifically in the Land. However, on the other hand it is stated (ibid. 11:16-18): "Take heed to yourselves lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods and bow down to them. And the anger of the Lord will be kindled against you … and you will perish quickly from the good land that the Lord is giving you. [And even so, also when you are in exile] you shall place these words of Mine upon your heart and upon your soul, and you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as totafot between your eyes." Thus even in exile there is a mitzva to fulfil the mitzvot. The Sages explained that the mitzvot that are dependent on the Land, that is, those connected to the soil, are to be fulfilled only in the Land, while the mitzvot that are not dependent on the Land must be fulfilled in exile as well, so that we will remember them and know how to fulfil them when we return to the Land. Moreover, through fulfilling them we will be roused to repentance and will merit bringing our redemption closer (Yerushalmi Shevi'it 6:1; Kiddushin 1:8; Bavli Kiddushin 37a; Sifrei Ekev 43-44).

These are the mitzvot dependent on the Land: ḥalla, orla, kilayim of seeds, kilayim of the vineyard, ḥadash, leket, shikheḥa, pe'a, peret, olelot, bikkurim, terumot and ma'asrot, reshit ha-gez (the first shearing), shevi'it and yovel. According to many, also the gifts of the foreleg, the cheeks and the maw (below, 15). And although the primary obligation of these mitzvot is in the Land, the obligation of many of them extends to some degree outside the Land as well (as explained in the note). There are also many other communal mitzvot that are dependent on the Land, such as establishing a judicial system, and many more mitzvot that depend on the building of the Temple and its existence, and we will not deal with any of these in this chapter.1

The obligation of all the mitzvot dependent on the Land of Israel depends also on the people of Israel, for the obligation of all of them began only after the people of Israel entered the main part of the Land, that is, the western side of the Jordan, which is the land of the seven Canaanite nations. The Torah obligation of shevi'it and yovel depends on the people dwelling in its Land in the proper manner, each tribe in its inheritance (below, 14). And the Torah obligation of ḥalla, terumot and ma'asrot depends on the majority of the people being in the Land (below, halakhot 2, 10, 11).

notes_en.en:
Orla – it is a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai (a law given to Moshe at Sinai) that it applies outside the Land as well, except that in the Land one must be stringent in a case of doubt, whereas outside the Land one is lenient (above, 2:1). Kilayim of the vineyard – by rabbinic law it is observed outside the Land as well, but only in its severe form that is agreed upon by all opinions (above, 3:4). Terumot and ma'asrot – the Sages instituted that they be observed in four lands adjacent to the Land, and now their obligation has lapsed (below, 13). Leket, shikheḥa and pe'a – the Sages instituted that they be observed outside the Land as well when there is a need for this for the Jewish poor (below, 15). The mitzva of ḥalla applies by rabbinic law outside the Land as well (below, 10). Shevi'it depends on the Land, but the remission of debts (shemitat kesafim) does not depend on the soil and applies outside the Land as well (Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it 6:1). Regarding the mitzva of ḥadash the Tanna'im disagreed, and the halakha was ruled that its obligation applies by Torah law outside the Land as well (Kiddushin 37a; above, 1:5), but only after entering the Land did they become obligated in the mitzva. Also the time at which grain becomes permitted is according to its growing season in the Land (above, 1:2), and the prohibition of harvesting ḥadash applies only in the Land (above, 1:4).
Let us mention briefly the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land: the mitzva of settling the Land with all that it entails, such as the war to conquer it, "They shall not dwell in your land," "and you shall not show them favour," the cities of the Levites and the cities of refuge, and the eradication of idolatry. Appointing a king or another leadership whose status is like that of a king. Appointing judges and officers in all the gates of Israel. Ordination of judges, sanctification of the months, intercalation of years, the egla arufa (the heifer whose neck is broken) and the zaken mamre (the rebellious elder). Building the Temple and the sacrificial service. Houses in walled cities, tzara'at of houses, and the ir ha-niddaḥat (the idolatrous city).

sections.body_en:
From the time Israel entered the Land they became obligated in the mitzvot that are incumbent on each individual for himself, and these are: ḥadash, orla, kilayim of seeds and kilayim of the vineyard. The land on which these mitzvot took effect is the land that those who came up from Egypt were commanded to conquer on the western side of the Jordan, as explained in Parashat Mas'ei (Bamidbar 34), and from the moment Israel crossed the Jordan the obligation took effect over all of it, even though in practice they had not yet conquered it. And since even before that they had conquered the eastern side of the Jordan, the obligation extended to it as well. But territories outside the boundary of those who came up from Egypt, even though they are within the borders of the Land of Israel – from the River of Egypt to the river Euphrates – did not become obligated in these mitzvot, as long as they had not been conquered by the people of Israel as a whole.2

In the mitzvot connected to the community, that is, terumot and ma'asrot, which are given by the owners of the fields to the kohanim, the Levites and the poor, and likewise shevi'it and yovel, which include all of Israel, they became obligated only after they had finished conquering the Land and dividing it among the tribes. The conquest lasted seven years, and the division into tribes and inheritances, until every person in Israel received his inheritance, lasted another seven years. It follows that in the fifteenth year after their entry into the Land they began to count years for shemita and yovel and to separate terumot and ma'asrot and to leave the gifts for the poor, and in the twenty-first year they observed the first shemita, and in the sixty-fourth year they observed the first yovel (Sifrei Ekev 41; Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 5:1).3

Until the Temple in Jerusalem was built, they would eat the produce of ma'aser sheni and neta revai near the Mishkan at Shilo (Mishna Zevaḥim 14:4-8), and it was there that they would bring up the bikkurim. So it continued for the 369 years of its existence. After that the Mishkan stood for another 57 years in Nov and Giv'on, and from there they went up to Jerusalem, to the Temple built by Shlomo, which stood for 410 years (Zevaḥim 118b; Rambam, Hilkhot Beit Ha-beḥira 1:2).

notes_en.en:
The obligation from the time they entered the Land is explained regarding ḥadash (Kiddushin 37b), ḥalla (Nidda 47a) and orla (Mishna Orla 1:2), and the same applies to kilayim, whose law is like that of orla. The individual mitzvot dependent on the Land, such as orla and kilayim, took effect on the boundary of those who came up from Egypt, which they were commanded to conquer, and not on the entire boundary of the Land of Israel. Their obligation continues from then on forever, since their obligation began the moment they crossed the Jordan, even before they actually conquered the Land, and therefore it also did not lapse at the time of the destruction (Yeshu'ot Malko, Terumot 1:26; Malbushei Yom Tov; She'ilat David; Kerem Tziyon; Gevulot Ha-sadeh 1:13). However, some hold that the obligation of the individual mitzvot also lapsed with the first destruction, and through the second sanctity they again became obligated by Torah law forever within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia (Maharit 1:47; Mor U-ketzi'a OḤ 306; Arukh Ha-shulḥan YD 294:10). And there is one who says that according to those who hold that the second sanctity lapsed, the obligation of orla and kilayim in our time is also rabbinic (Mishneh La-melekh). And there is one who holds that even in the time of the Second Temple the obligation of orla was rabbinic, because for it too the verse requires that the majority of its inhabitants be upon it (Tzlaḥ, Berakhot 36a). The main view is that of most poskim, that their obligation is by Torah law from the days of Yehoshua bin Nun forever, throughout the boundary of those who came up from Egypt. And in Syria and outside the Land, orla is from a "halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai," and kilayim of the vineyard is by rabbinic law (see Mishna Orla 3:9).
Regarding the gifts for the poor that are left for the poor there is a doubt (below, halakha 15), since on the one hand they are left for the poor, and there is a communal aspect to this as with shevi'it, and on the other hand it is a personal obligation to leave them in the field, and they are not similar to shevi'it, where the whole Land must rest.

The obligation of shevi'it and yovel depends on the completion of the division of the Land into inheritances, as explained in Sifra, Vayikra 25:3; Arakhin 32b; Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 5:1. The order of becoming obligated in the mitzvot dependent on the Land according to the years is explained in Tosefta Menaḥot 6:20; Rambam, Hilkhot Shemita Ve-yovel 10:2; Peninei Halakha, ibid.
The obligation of terumot and ma'asrot began at the completion of the division of the Land, when every person in Israel had received his inheritance, as explained in Nidda 47a and Ketubot 25a, and there in Rashi, s.v. "ve-lo nitḥayvu," it is explained that the mitzva of terumot and ma'asrot depends on the counting of the years of shemita, for in years 1, 2, 4 and 5 one separates ma'aser sheni, and in years 3 and 6 ma'aser ani, and in shemita one renounces ownership of the produce and is exempt from terumot and ma'asrot.

sections.body_en:
Beyond the borders conquered by Moshe and Yehoshua, in which the twelve tribes received their inheritances, King David conquered Syria, including territories within the borders of the Land of Israel such as Aram Damascus, and territories outside the borders of the Land, such as Aram Naharayim between the Euphrates and the Tigris. His conquest was meant to subdue enemies who might threaten Israel in the future, and instead of hostile kingdoms developing there, David stationed governors there who collected tribute from them to strengthen his kingdom (II Shmuel 8:3-13; 10:16-19). The Sages said that this conquest was not carried out in the proper order, since the mitzva was first to conquer the entire land of Canaan within the borders explained in Parashat Mas'ei (Bamidbar 34), and he conquered Syria before he conquered Jerusalem, which was ruled by the Jebusites (Sifrei Ekev 51). Apparently David departed from the order because he did not intend to designate Syria for Jewish settlement, since at that time the people of Israel had not yet properly filled the territories it had inherited in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun. And he held that if he conquered Syria in order to subdue enemies and collect tribute from them to strengthen his kingdom, this is not considered a departure from the proper order. Therefore his conquest is called a "kibush yaḥid" (an individual's conquest), which was carried out to strengthen his kingdom and not in order to settle the Land.

Since the conquest was not in the proper order, a doubt arose regarding its status. According to Rabbi Meir, although Syria was conquered by an individual's conquest, there is a Torah obligation to fulfil the mitzvot dependent on the Land there. Therefore one is obligated by Torah law to separate terumot and ma'asrot in Syria, and it is forbidden to sell a house there to a gentile. According to Rabbi Yosei, since it was conquered by an individual's conquest, it became obligated in the mitzvot dependent on the Land only by rabbinic law, including the mitzva of terumot and ma'asrot, and in a time of need it is permitted to sell a house there to a gentile. And so the halakha was ruled (Gittin 8a-b; Avoda Zara 21a; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 10:3). However, even according to Rabbi Yosei, since all the territories up to the river Euphrates are within the borders of the Land of Israel, there is a mitzva to settle them and to buy houses in them, and even on Shabbat a Jew is permitted to transgress a rabbinic prohibition of "shevut" in order to buy a house there (Rambam, Hilkhot Shabbat 6:11).4

notes_en.en:
In Sifrei Ekev 51 it is explained that David "acted not in accordance with the Torah," which commanded first to conquer the entire land of Canaan and Jerusalem, and he conquered Syria before he conquered the Jebusites who dwelt on Mount Moriah, near his palace in the City of David; therefore the status of Syria is an intermediate status (and so it is brought in Tosafot Rashba and Ritva). The Sages called his conquest a "kibush yaḥid." Rashi explained (Gittin 8b) that this was because all of Israel was not there together, and he conquered it for his own needs and not for the needs of the people of Israel as a whole. It seems that his intent is that he did not conquer it for the sake of settling the Land, but in order to raise tribute to strengthen his kingdom, as is clear from the verses stating that David stationed governors there (II Shmuel 8:6).
In accordance with the words of the Sifrei, Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Terumot 1:3) that Syria was not sanctified like the Land of Israel, because he had not yet conquered the entire land of the seven nations, which is the land of Canaan, and this even though he conquered Syria by authority of the beit din. Some Rishonim wrote that David conquered it not by authority of the beit din (Ramban, Devarim 11:24; Ritva, Avoda Zara 21a). It seems that they do not disagree; rather, presumably he consulted the Sanhedrin before he conquered Syria, as he was always accustomed to do (see Berakhot 3b), in accordance with the words of Rambam. However, he consulted regarding the security aspect and not regarding the order of conquering and settling the Land. And although his intention and his actions were desirable, a problem was created, since he departed from the order, and it was not clear whether there was an intention to settle Syria. Therefore halakhic complications also arose.
It is explained in Rambam (Hilkhot Terumot 1:3-4, 9) that the law of Syria extends to the territory within the Land, whose border reaches the river Euphrates, including the entire territory of Aram Damascus, and also to the territories outside the Land, including Aram Naharayim beyond the river Euphrates and north of Hor Ha-har in the north of Aram Tzova (Peninei Halakha: The Nation and the Land 3:16). Had he first conquered all the borders of Mas'ei, the territories outside the Land would also have become sanctified, as it is stated (Devarim 11:24): "Every place on which the sole of your foot shall tread shall be yours," and as explained in the Sifrei there (Ekev 51).
According to all opinions, the status of Syria is an intermediate status (Ramban, Devarim 11:24), since it is explained in Gittin 8a-b that even according to the view that an individual's conquest is effective by Torah law, with respect to three matters that the Sages instituted, Syria is equivalent to outside the Land, and the decree of impurity that they decreed on outside the Land applies to Syria as well. And even according to Rabbi Yosei, who holds that an individual's conquest is not a conquest, and the halakha follows him (Avoda Zara 21a; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 10:3), one is obligated to separate terumot and ma'asrot there by rabbinic law. Except that since the obligation is rabbinic, ownership by a gentile cancels the obligation there, even if the processing of the produce was completed in the hands of a Jew (Gittin 47a; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 1:4, 15). And even according to Rabbi Yosei there is a mitzva to buy a house in Syria for the sake of settling the Land (Rambam, Hilkhot Shabbat 6:11), and in my humble opinion the intent is to the part within the border of the Land. Regarding ma'aser sheni in Syria there is a disagreement: according to Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni 1:14) and SA (331:131), since it is not possible to bring ma'aser sheni up from Syria to eat it in Jerusalem, for the law of ma'aser sheni is like the law of a firstborn animal, they did not institute separating "ma'aser sheni" in Syria. On the other hand, according to Ra'avad, Rashba and the Gra (331:197), in Syria too one is obligated to separate ma'aser sheni, and they would redeem it and bring its money up to Jerusalem.

sections.title_en: The Days of Exile and the First Destruction
sections.body_en:
From the time the members of the tribes of Re'uven, Gad and half of Menashe were exiled (in the year 3188 from the creation of the world), about a hundred and fifty years before the destruction, the mitzvot of shevi'it and yovel lapsed by Torah law, as it is stated (Vayikra 25:10): "And you shall proclaim liberty in the land to all its inhabitants" – "at a time when all its inhabitants are upon it, and not at a time when some of them have been exiled"; and when the obligation of yovel lapses, the obligation of shevi'it lapses as well (Arakhin 32b; Gittin 36a. The reason is explained in Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 1:9; 5:3).

They were still obligated in the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot by Torah law, and although they observed the mitzva of shevi'it by rabbinic law or by custom, the counting of the shemita years, on which the obligation of the tithes depended, continued by Torah law (see Rambam, Hilkhot Shemita Ve-yovel 10:5; and see Tosafot, Arakhin 12b, s.v. "hanakh shnei").

About eighteen years later (in the year 3206 from the creation of the world), the Torah obligation of ḥalla and of terumot and ma'asrot lapsed, since the majority of Israel was no longer in its Land. And from the time the First Temple was destroyed, the sanctity that forms the basis for the obligation of all the mitzvot fulfilled by the community lapsed, such as ḥalla and teruma, which are given to the kohanim; ma'aser rishon, which is given to the Levites; ma'aser sheni, which all of Israel eats in Jerusalem; ma'aser ani, which is given to the poor; and shevi'it and yovel, which depend on all the tribes of Israel being in their inheritances. For since these mitzvot depend on the situation of the people of Israel as a whole, the foundation of their obligation lapsed at the time of the destruction. This is what the Sages said (Ḥullin 7a): "The first sanctity sanctified for its time but did not sanctify for the future," meaning that the first sanctity lapsed with the destruction of the First Temple.

But in the mitzvot fulfilled by each individual for himself, such as orla and kilayim, one is obligated by Torah law even after the destruction of the Temple and the exile of Israel. For since their obligation began from the time they entered the Land, even before they conquered it and divided its inheritances, the destruction and the exile do not cancel their obligation.5

notes_en.en:
The mitzvot that are fulfilled by the community depend on Israel's sanctification of the Land, through conquest as in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun, or through settlement as in the days of Ezra, as explained in Rambam (Hilkhot Terumot 1:2, 5; Hilkhot Beit Ha-beḥira 6:16). With regard to shevi'it and yovel, it is also necessary that the majority of each tribe dwell in its inheritance (Arakhin 32b), and therefore their Torah obligation lapsed at the time of the exile of the tribes of Re'uven and Gad. And according to those who hold that Yirmeyahu brought the ten tribes back to dwell in their inheritance, their Torah obligation returned then (Arakhin 33a; and see Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 5, note 3). The Torah obligation of the mitzva of ḥalla depends on the majority of Israel being in the Land (below, 10), and therefore it lapsed before the destruction, at the time of the exile of the ten tribes. Regarding terumot and ma'asrot there is a disagreement. According to many Rishonim, the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot lapsed at the time of the destruction (Rashi, Ra'avad, Rashba, Ran and many others). According to Rambam, the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot, like ḥalla, also depends on the majority of Israel and lapsed with the exile of the ten tribes (Hilkhot Terumot 1:26). And so I wrote above, since this is the view of most Aḥaronim. It seems that according to Rambam too, the foundation of the obligation lapsed only at the time of the destruction. For until the destruction, had the majority of Israel returned to the Land, the Torah obligation of ḥalla and of terumot and ma'asrot would have returned without any special act of sanctification, even if they were under foreign rule. But once the First Temple was destroyed, even if the majority of Israel had returned, without an additional sanctification the Torah obligation would not have returned (Mahari Kurkus, Hilkhot Shemita Ve-yovel 12:15; Derekh Emuna, Terumot 1:51).
The foundation of the second sanctity is the first sanctity, as can be learned from the law of walled cities, which were sanctified in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun, and their sanctity determines that houses sold in them become the permanent property of the buyer after one year and do not return to their owners in the yovel. There is also a mitzva to send a metzora out of them, and it is forbidden to sow their open lands (a thousand amot in each direction). In Arakhin 32b the Tanna'im disagreed: some say that those who came up from Babylonia did not need to sanctify them again, because "the first sanctity sanctified for its time and sanctified for the future." And some say: "When the members of the exile came up, they found these (the cities that had been sanctified the first time) and sanctified them, but the first ones lapsed once the sanctity of the Land lapsed." It seems that even according to their view, the first sanctity, which was effected by force of the conquest, was the basis upon which the second sanctification, effected by force of the settlement, took place, and as the Aḥaronim explained, Ezra could sanctify only cities that Yehoshua bin Nun had already sanctified (Turei Even, Megilla 10a; Mishneh La-melekh, Hilkhot Shemita Ve-yovel 12:15; Derekh Emuna there, in Be'ur Ha-halakha, s.v. "keyvan." And see Minḥat Ḥinukh 340:1, s.v. "u-mevu'ar").

sections.title_en: The Prophets' Enactment of Terumot and Ma'asrot in Babylonia
sections.body_en:
At the end of the days of the First Temple, after the exile of Yehoyakhin, when a community of exiles began to form in Babylonia, the prophets instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated also from the produce that grows in Shin'ar, which is Babylonia, because it is adjacent to the Land of Israel and many Jews would go and settle there. The enactment was meant to preserve the values of the mitzva among the exiles and to help the poor. And perhaps they were also concerned that there would be Jews who would prefer to leave the Land in order to be exempt from the obligation to separate twenty percent of the crop for terumot and ma'asrot; therefore they instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated in Babylonia as well. And since there is no mitzva of shevi'it in Babylonia, they instituted that in shevi'it too terumot and ma'asrot be separated, and that "ma'aser sheni" be separated (as will be explained below, 13).

Apparently they continued to separate terumot and ma'asrot in Babylonia even after the destruction of the Temple, and they continued counting the shemita cycles, since it is the basis for the order of separating terumot and ma'asrot, for in years 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 they separated "ma'aser sheni," and in years 3 and 6 "ma'aser ani" (see Rambam, Hilkhot Shemita Ve-yovel 10:5). However, in the Land the obligation lapsed, and presumably there were those who separated terumot and ma'asrot as a matter of custom, but they were not obligated to do so, until the Men of the Great Assembly returned and sanctified the Land a second time.

Even after the Land was restored and sanctified a second time, the enactment of the prophets remained in place. And the elders who led Israel after Ezra the Scribe further instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated in Egypt as well, since there too there was a large Jewish community. Except that they instituted that in shevi'it "ma'aser ani" be separated in Egypt, so that the poor of the Land could be helped by it during shevi'it. Afterwards they likewise instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated in the lands of Amon and Moav, and it was ruled that in shevi'it "ma'aser ani" be separated (Mishna Yadayim 4:3).6

notes_en.en:
Apparently, the Babylonian exile had a Torah standing that could have competed with Jerusalem, and it was necessary to tie it more closely to Jerusalem; therefore they instituted that in shevi'it "ma'aser sheni" be separated and its redemption money be brought up to Jerusalem (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni 1:14). However, the exile in Egypt, at the time of the enactment, did not have standing in competition with Jerusalem, and likewise the exile in Amon and Moav. On the other hand, they were closer to the Land of Israel, and therefore they instituted that in shevi'it "ma'aser ani" be separated, thereby helping the poor of the Land of Israel.
During the years of the destruction, the mitzva to eat from the money of "ma'aser sheni" in Jerusalem lapsed, since it depends on the altar. Perhaps in those years they were accustomed to destroy the produce of "ma'aser sheni," but it is more likely that they redeemed it onto a peruta, since that was its true value.

sections.title_en: Accepting the Torah in the Days of Ezra
sections.body_en:
Fifty-two years after the destruction of the First Temple, Koresh king of Persia gave permission to the Jews of Babylonia to return to the Land and build the Temple. But only 42 thousand volunteered and went up to the Land. The returnees settled in Jerusalem and its surroundings, built the altar and offered sacrifices on it, and prepared to build the Temple. However, following letters of accusation that the gentiles of the land sent to the Persian kingdom, the building of the Temple was halted for 18 years, until Daryavesh II, the son of Aḥashverosh and Queen Esther, permitted the building of the Temple (Megilla 11b-12a, and Rashi there).

However, the national and spiritual situation of the people of Israel was still at a low ebb. The overwhelming majority of the people preferred to remain in exile, and the Jewish community in the Land was small in number and poor in spirit. Few engaged in Torah study, many mitzvot were neglected, and even among the sons of the kohanim many sinned and married foreign women. They apparently thought that in the new reality, in which the people of Israel was scattered and dispersed among the nations, there was no longer an obligation to observe the mitzvot. It was then clear that, in view of the new era, it was necessary to establish how the Torah would continue to be fulfilled in Israel.

In the sixth year after the building of the Temple, the spiritual giant Ezra the Scribe came up from Babylonia and began to rouse the people to engage in Torah and to fulfil the mitzvot. Regarding Ezra's greatness the Sages said (Sanhedrin 21b): "Ezra was worthy that the Torah be given through him, had Moshe not preceded him." They also said (Sukka 20a): "When the Torah was forgotten from Israel, Ezra came up from Babylonia and re-established it." In addition to being a sage he was also a prophet, and his prophetic name was Malakhi (Megilla 15a). About 13 years after Ezra's ascent, the official Neḥemya came up to Jerusalem, holding governmental authority from the king of Persia, and together with Ezra he established the Jewish community in the Land both nationally and religiously.

The Sages said that the coming of Israel to the Land in the days of Ezra the Scribe is compared to their coming in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun: just as in their coming in the days of Yehoshua they accepted the mitzvot upon themselves, so too in their coming in the days of Ezra. And just as those who came up from Egypt were commanded that after their entry into the Land, at the assembly at Mount Gerizim and Mount Eival, they should again make a covenant on the Torah they had received at Sinai (Devarim 11:29-32; 27:1-26), so too they had to make a covenant on it again in the days of Ezra (Yerushalmi Shevi'it 6:1; Bavli Arakhin 32b).

And so indeed it is related in Scripture that in the days of Ezra and Neḥemya, Israel accepted upon themselves to observe the Torah, emphasizing the mitzvot that needed strengthening. As it is stated (Neḥemya 10:1-40): "And because of all this we make a firm covenant and write it, and on the sealed document are our princes, our Levites and our priests. And on the sealed documents (the fathers' houses of the kohanim and the Levites, and the heads of the people) … and they enter into a curse and into an oath to walk in God's Torah, which was given by Moshe the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the Lord our Lord, and His ordinances and His statutes; and that we will not give our daughters to the peoples of the land (the gentiles), nor take their daughters for our sons; and if the peoples of the land bring wares or any grain on the Sabbath day to sell, we will not buy from them on the Sabbath or on a holy day (not to trade on Shabbat and festivals); and that we will forgo the seventh year (to rest in shevi'it), and the exaction of every debt (the remission of debts) … and to bring the first fruits of our ground and the first fruits of all fruit of every tree, year by year, to the house of the Lord; and the firstborn of our sons and of our cattle, as it is written in the Torah, and the firstlings of our herds and of our flocks, to bring to the house of our God, to the priests who minister in the house of our God; and that we should bring the first of our dough (ḥalla) and our terumot, and the fruit of every tree, wine and oil, to the priests, to the chambers of the house of our God, and the tithes of our ground to the Levites …"

In order to establish the Torah in Israel, Ezra the Scribe founded the great beit din, the most important in the history of Israel, which was called the "Great Assembly," and in it were members one hundred and twenty sages, among them the last of the prophets. This beit din examined the state of Judaism and established enactments through which the people of Israel would be able to survive even while dispersed, part of it in the Land and most of it outside the Land. Among other things, the Men of the Great Assembly instituted the text of the prayers and blessings, the times of the Torah reading in the synagogues, and the times at which the courts would sit to judge between man and his fellow. Through these enactments the Men of the Great Assembly restored the Torah in Israel and laid the foundation for the continued building of the Oral Torah, by raising up many students, and by paving the way for the sages of Israel in the coming generations to enact enactments and establish safeguards according to the needs of the generation.7

notes_en.en:
All agree that according to the view of the Sages (Arakhin 12b-13a), at the end of the sixth year after the establishment of the Temple, Ezra came up and sanctified the Land for its mitzvot, and in the seventh year they began to count years for shemita and yovel. And all agree that about 13 years later Neḥemya came up and helped Ezra to establish his enterprise. However, regarding the time of the covenant (Neḥemya 8-10) there is perplexity and disagreement (see Malbim, Neḥemya 7:73; and Harḥavot here). In my humble opinion, Ezra and Neḥemya came up with Zerubavel eighteen years before the establishment of the Temple and were young at the time, and Ezra then served as scribe for the elders who made the covenant, and afterwards he returned to Babylonia to study Torah with his teacher Barukh ben Neriya (Megilla 16b). Neḥemya too returned to serve in the Persian royal court. Twenty-four years after Zerubavel's ascent, after the death of Barukh ben Neriya, in the sixth year after the establishment of the Temple, Ezra the Scribe came up to the Land and became the spiritual leader of Israel, convened the Great Assembly and sealed its enactments, establishing the text of the prayer and the blessings and the order of the years for shemita and yovel, and after him Neḥemya came up and strengthened his enterprise. And the covenant mentioned in the verses combines within it all the covenants that were accepted over the course of those generations.
If, as a custom, they continued to count shemita cycles after the first destruction without yovel years, it follows that when they resumed counting years in the days of Ezra they continued the custom, and only in the fiftieth year did they add a yovel (according to the view of the Sages, Nedarim 61a). And according to Rashi's version (Avoda Zara 9b), even according to the view of Rabbi Yehuda they continued the custom. However, according to Rabbeinu Tam's version (Arakhin 12b), according to the view of Rabbi Yehuda, when they resumed counting shevi'it the previous custom lapsed and they began a new order (see Harḥavot).

sections.title_en: The Second Sanctity and Its Force for the Communal Mitzvot
sections.body_en:
One of the harshest expressions of the crisis that befell the people of Israel following the destruction of the First Temple was the cancellation of the obligation to fulfil the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land, such as shemita and yovel, terumot and ma'asrot and the gifts for the poor – the mitzvot through which the divine values find expression in practical public life, and through which the unique character of the people of Israel is revealed. Presumably, even after the destruction there were still Jews who continued to fulfil these mitzvot to some extent. But they did so as an ancestral custom and not because they were obligated in them. The crowning achievement of the work of Ezra the Scribe was restoring these mitzvot to their force. In the seventh year after the establishment of the Temple, Ezra and his beit din again sanctified the Land for its mitzvot, and began to count years for shemita and yovel, and Israel again became obligated in the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot, ḥalla, the gifts for the poor and shevi'it.

The Sages said that the first sanctity, with which the Land was sanctified for the communal mitzvot in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun, was sanctified for its time and lapsed at the time of the destruction. But the second sanctity, with which the Land was sanctified in the days of Ezra, remained forever. For it is stated in the Torah that after we sin and the punishment of exile is fulfilled in us, God will bring us back to our Land a second time, as it is stated (Devarim 30:3-5): "Then the Lord your God will bring back your captivity and have compassion on you, and will return and gather you from all the peoples where the Lord your God has scattered you … And the Lord your God will bring you into the land which your fathers possessed, and you shall possess it …" The Sages said: "which [your fathers] possessed" – this is the first coming, in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun; "and you shall possess it" – this is the second coming, in the days of Ezra. And since the Torah does not mention that there will be a further possession, it follows that by force of the second possession the Land will remain sanctified forever, and even after the destruction of the Second Temple it will not lapse (Yevamot 82b). For the first sanctity lapsed because it was effected through conquest, and therefore when the Land was taken from us and the conquest ended, the sanctity lapsed. But the second sanctity was effected through Israel settling in the Land and holding on to it despite all the difficulties. And since the sanctity took effect through settlement even though Israel did not have sovereignty, it is based on the claim of right of the people of Israel to its Land, which rests on the divine promise, and since the claim of right never lapses, the destruction and the exile too did not cancel the sanctity of the Land for its mitzvot (based on Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 1:5; Hilkhot Beit Ha-beḥira 6:16). It seems that the first sanctity was the basis for the second sanctity, since the sanctity of the Land for its mitzvot is actualized in its fullness through the mitzva of settling the Land in both its parts, conquest and settlement, as it is stated (Devarim 11:31): "and you shall possess it and dwell in it" – possession is conquest, and dwelling is settlement. And after the people of Israel acquired its Land through both parts of the mitzva, the Land remained sanctified for its mitzvot forever.

Admittedly, there are Rishonim who disagree and hold that the second sanctity also lapsed after the destruction (Rashba, Ritva and Ran), but it is accepted in halakha that the second sanctity never lapses.8

notes_en.en:
From the words of Rabbi Yoḥanan (Yevamot 82b) it is implied that there is a disagreement about this: according to Rabbi Yosei, who is the Tanna who taught the midrash "Seder Olam," the second sanctity sanctified for its time and for the future, and therefore the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot in our time is by Torah law; whereas according to the Sages in the baraita (ibid. 82a), teruma in our time is rabbinic, because they do not agree with Rabbi Yosei that the second sanctity sanctified for the future. Some Rishonim hold that the halakha follows the Sages, and the second sanctity lapsed with the destruction, and therefore the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot after the destruction is rabbinic (Rashba, Ritva, Ran, Sefer Ha-teruma and Tashbetz). Other Rishonim hold that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, and the second sanctity did not lapse, and therefore the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot today is by Torah law (Rashi, Ra'avad, Tur in the name of Ri, and Kaftor Va-feraḥ). The view of Rambam is that the second sanctity did not lapse, but the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot is rabbinic because the majority of Israel is not in the Land. And one can say that according to Rambam, even the Sages who disagreed with Rabbi Yosei agree that the second sanctity did not lapse, but Rabbi Yoḥanan explained that according to them terumot and ma'asrot are rabbinic, because their Torah obligation depends on the majority of Israel dwelling in the Land (as explained in Nidda 47a). And so it was ruled in Rambam (Hilkhot Terumot 1:26). And so it appears from Semag (positive commandment 133), Ḥinukh (507), Maggid Mishneh (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 20:3) and Maharit (1:25). And so it is agreed by nearly all the Aḥaronim that the second sanctity was sanctified forever, except that in practice the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot is by Torah law only when the majority of its inhabitants are upon it (Radbaz; SA 331:2; Arukh Ha-shulḥan).
In the Yerushalmi, Shevi'it (6:1), a baraita is cited: "It compared their coming in the days of Ezra to their coming in the days of Yehoshua: just as in their coming in the days of Yehoshua they were exempt and became obligated, so too in their coming in the days of Ezra they were exempt and became obligated." The Amora'im disagreed regarding the level of their obligation in the days of Ezra: according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Ḥanina, it was by Torah law. On the contrary, the fact that they accepted the mitzvot even though they were few, under foreign rule, and had not yet conquered the whole Land, is their merit, and about this it is stated (Devarim 30:5): "and He will do you good and multiply you more than your fathers." And perhaps it was precisely in this merit that their sanctity endured for generations, since through the efforts of settlement the right of Israel to its Land forever was established with greater force. See there. And according to Rabbi Elazar, they did not become obligated in the days of Ezra by Torah law; rather they accepted the mitzvot upon themselves by rabbinic law, and therefore they had to make a covenant of faith about it (Neḥemya 10:1, 33, 36-38). And the possession that will be of greater stature and will endure for generations will be in the future to come, when the Land will again be sanctified by Torah law. Until here [the Yerushalmi]. And it is implied that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar. However, many explained his view according to Rambam, that in the days of the Second Temple they were obligated in terumot and ma'asrot and in shemita and yovel by rabbinic law, because the majority of its inhabitants were not upon it and they did not dwell in their proper manner (Mahara Fulda, Penei Moshe and Rash Sirilio), but even Rabbi Elazar agrees that the very foundation of the second sanctity is by Torah law and for all generations, and when the majority of its inhabitants are upon it, the obligation of these mitzvot will take effect by Torah law without an additional sanctification. And according to the Rash (Shevi'it 6:1), according to all views, when they established the second sanctity they became obligated in terumot and ma'asrot by Torah law, except that according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Ḥanina they were obligated to sanctify the Land by Torah law as in the days of Yehoshua, and consequently its sanctity remained for generations, whereas according to Rabbi Elazar they were permitted to sanctify the Land by Torah law, and they sanctified it only for the period during which the Temple stood, and therefore after it was destroyed the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot is rabbinic, and at the third coming the obligation will again become Torah law without an additional sanctification (and this is the explanation of the view of Rashba, Ritva and Ran). And according to the Gra (331:6), the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar that the second sanctity was rabbinic, and it was sanctified for generations, as Rambam says. However, the Gra too agrees that there will be no need for a third sanctification, for by force of the second sanctity, when the majority of Israel is in the Land, we will be obligated in terumot and ma'asrot by Torah law. Above I wrote according to the views mentioned earlier, according to which the Land was sanctified with the second sanctity by Torah law, except that according to Rambam and those who agree with him, the obligation of shevi'it and of terumot and ma'asrot was rabbinic, because the majority of its inhabitants were not upon it.

sections.title_en: The Area of the Sanctity: Those Who Came Up from Babylonia and Those Who Came Up from Egypt
sections.body_en:
Since the second sanctity was established through settlement, it took effect on all the places in which Israel settled in the days of the Second Temple. As the boundary of settlement of those who came up from Babylonia expanded, so the boundary of the sanctity expanded, and these places are called the "boundary of those who came up from Babylonia." At first they settled in Yehuda and Binyamin, and over time, thanks to the Hasmonean kingdom, the continuing aliya and natural growth, the settlement expanded to Shomron, to the Lower and Upper Galilee, to the coastal plain from Ashkelon to Akko, to the Golan and to the eastern side of the Jordan.

When they sanctified the area of settlement, the sanctity was reawakened also in all the places that those who came up from Egypt had conquered on both sides of the Jordan, and it even spread to Syria, except that they determined that within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia the sanctity would take effect by Torah law, and within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and in Syria by rabbinic law. The Men of the Great Assembly could have determined that the sanctity would spread in full throughout the boundary of "those who came up from Egypt" and Syria, but they chose to leave the places that were not properly settled with a less severe obligation, in order to ease things somewhat for the poor. On the other hand, they could have determined that the sanctity would not apply at all to the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and to Syria, but they did not want to exempt them, so that there too the poor could benefit from terumot and ma'asrot and from the renunciation of produce in shevi'it. And even within the area of those who came up from Babylonia there were cities in which gentiles lived, such as Beit She'an and Ashkelon, and the Sages did not apply to them the full obligation of the mitzvot as in the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia (Ḥagiga 3b; Ḥullin 7a). In those days the law of the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and of those cities was known, but in time it was forgotten, and the poskim disagreed about it, as explained below (halakha 12).

In any case, after the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land for the communal mitzvot dependent on it, they no longer needed to sanctify again the places to which Jewish settlement spread in the days of the Second Temple; rather, the sanctity spread together with the settlement. And even after the destruction of the Second Temple, the sanctity remained throughout the area of those who came up from Babylonia, because a place that has already been sanctified with the second sanctity never again loses its sanctity. For we have learned (above, 7) that the Sages expounded that after the second sanctity, with which the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land, Israel will never again need to sanctify it. It follows, then, that what we said, that in the boundary of those who came up from Egypt the obligation of the communal mitzvot is rabbinic, refers to places in which there was no organized Jewish settlement during the days of the Second Temple.9

notes_en.en: The law of the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia, which applies to large territories, is explained in Tosefta Shevi'it 4:11; Sifrei Ekev 51; Yerushalmi Shevi'it 9:2. And although in the days of Ezra they settled only in a limited area around Jerusalem (Ezra chapter 2), we must say that the sanctity spread with the settlement, as they said in the Yerushalmi (Shevi'it 6:1): "Your fathers (in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun) did not become obligated until they had acquired all of it, but you – each one, as he acquires, becomes obligated" (and see Bava Metzia 28a). And although in the days of the Hasmonean kingdom the boundary of their kingdom spread beyond the area of settlement, these places were not sanctified for generations, since only the places that were properly settled by many Jews were sanctified for generations (so it is implied by Mor U-ketzi'a 306. And see Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it 5, end of note 7). It seems that from the sanctity with which the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia was sanctified, sanctity spread to some degree also to the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and to Syria, which were not settled by many Jews, and therefore the law of the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and of Syria remained pending the decision of the Sages, and they decided that in halakha too it would be at an intermediate level, in which the foundation of the obligation of the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land would apply there by rabbinic law. This is what they said (Ḥullin 7a): "They left them so that the poor could rely on them in shevi'it." On the one hand, they did not want to exempt the boundary of those who came up from Egypt from terumot and ma'asrot and shevi'it, so that there too the poor could benefit from terumot and ma'asrot and the resting of the land in shevi'it (see Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 1:5, and the commentators on it). On the other hand, in order to ease things for the poor, the field owners and those who gather ownerless produce, the Sages did not want to be stringent in all the laws that apply in the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia; therefore, when they enacted stringent enactments for the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia, such as sefiḥim (aftergrowths) and demai, they did not apply them to the boundary of those who came up from Egypt (see Kaftor Va-feraḥ, chapter 5).

sections.title_en: The Decree of Impurity on the Land of the Nations
sections.body_en:
In the days of the Second Temple the Sages decreed impurity on the "land of the nations," that is, on the places outside the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia in which there was no Jewish settlement. The reason for the decree was that the gentiles would bury their dead in the ground without a grave, and sometimes the bones of their dead would become scattered, broken and mixed with the earth until it was difficult to distinguish them. And the halakha is that a bone of a corpse, whether of a Jew or of a gentile, even the size of a barley grain, renders one who touches it impure. Therefore they decreed that anyone who touches the earth of the land of the nations is considered as having touched a corpse and becomes impure.

An additional reason accompanied the decree: to prevent Israel from leaving the boundary of settlement, in which the essential fulfilment of the mitzva of settling the Land takes place. For this was the aim – that the second sanctity spread gradually with continuous Jewish settlement, and not that Jews scatter among the gentiles without the Land being considered theirs. And indeed we find that this decree was effective, and thanks to it they refrained from leaving the area of Jewish settlement even for a short time. Not only that, but they even called the places outside the area of Jewish settlement "outside the Land" and "the land of the nations," even though they are in the Land of Israel (Gittin 76b).10

Since kohanim are forbidden to become impure through a corpse, after the decree of impurity on the land of the nations, kohanim were forbidden to leave the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia. Only when they had a great need, such as to save property, to marry a wife or to study Torah, were they permitted to leave (Avoda Zara 13a). Today, when purity is not practised, kohanim are permitted to leave the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia, and what remains is the general prohibition on every Jew to leave the Land of Israel for outside the Land.11

notes_en.en:
A fragment of bone, even only the size of a barley grain, imparts corpse impurity through contact and through carrying, but it does not impart impurity through a tent (ohel). And since the gentiles were not careful in the burial of their dead, and their bones were broken and scattered, they decreed regarding the earth of the land of the nations, that is, all the earth in the places where gentiles lived, including the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and Syria, that it be an avi avot ha-tum'a (a primary source of impurity), so that anyone who touches it or carries it becomes impure for seven days, and becomes pure through sprinkling of the water of the ashes of the red heifer on the third and seventh days, immersion, and ha'arev shemesh (waiting until the end of the day), and teruma that touched it is burned (Mishna Ohalot 2:3; Shabbat 15b; Rambam, Hilkhot Tum'at Met 2:16; 11:1-2).
There was another fundamental reason for the decree: to prevent Israel from leaving for outside the Land. This is what the Tanna'im disagreed about in the Mishna (Ḥalla 4:7): according to Rabbi Eliezer this impurity applies only outside the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and Syria – thus the decree was so that they would not leave the places in which they fulfilled the mitzva of settling the Land through a conquest of the many and of an individual, even though gentiles lived in the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and there too there was concern of a corpse's bone. And according to Rabban Gamliel, whom the halakha follows, the decree was on everything outside the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia. It seems that according to Rabban Gamliel too, the mitzva of settling the Land stood at the basis of the decree, since the essence of the mitzva is that the Land be settled by us, and therefore it is fulfilled through settlement, which must be expanded gradually to the entire Land of Israel, and therefore they did not want Jews to leave the areas of settlement. And so we find in Gittin 76b that the Sages refrained from going beyond Akko "because it is forbidden to leave the Land for outside the Land," yet the area north of Akko is also the Land of Israel! Rather, they meant that it is forbidden to leave the boundary of settlement, in which the mitzva of settling the Land is fulfilled properly. (Since the boundary of those who came up from Egypt was not properly settled by Jews, there were no batei din in it that supervised halakhic matters, and therefore they instituted that an agent who brings a get from the boundary of those who came up from Egypt must testify that the get was written and signed in his presence, and without this the get is not to be accepted, lest it was not written and signed according to halakha, as explained in Gittin 2a-b.)
However, actually leaving for outside the Land is more severe; therefore they further decreed impurity on the air of outside the Land. Hence one who rode on an animal and did not touch the ground in the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and Syria did not become impure, but if he reached outside the Land, he became impure from the air. This impurity is light, and to become pure from it immersion and "ha'arev shemesh" suffice. And teruma that went out into the air of outside the Land is neither eaten nor burned (Gittin 8a; Rambam, Hilkhot Tum'at Met 11:1-2; and see Tosafot, Nazir 54b, s.v. "eretz"; Mishneh La-melekh, Hilkhot Tum'at Met 11:1; Kol Mevaser 1:63).
It is worth adding that even within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia, a place where gentiles lived was impure out of doubt, lest they had buried stillborn infants there, and these places were called "dwellings of gentiles" (Mishna Ohalot 18:7; Rambam, ibid. 11:7). And after it became clear that the Kutim worshipped idols, they decreed impurity on their land in Shomron as well, as in the boundary of those who came up from Egypt (see Ḥagiga 25a, Tosafot, s.v. "she-retzu'a"; and in Kaftor Va-feraḥ chapter 10 he explained that their impurity was because of stillborn infants – "dwellings of gentiles" – and not because of the land of the nations).

Some say that even today, when purity is not practised, kohanim are forbidden to leave the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia, just as they are forbidden to become impure through a corpse even though they are already impure. So wrote Rambam (Hilkhot Evel 3:14), SA (YD 372:1; 369:1) and Shvut Ya'akov (2:98). However, the Maharshal (YD 369) wrote that the prohibition of leaving the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia applied only when the kohanim kept themselves in purity, but today, when all are impure through corpses, this law too has lapsed. And so wrote there the Perisha, Baḥ, Shakh, Taz, Rabbi Akiva Eiger in the name of Mahariksh; Ḥokhmat Adam, Sha'ar Ha-simḥa 159:1. And since the basis of the impurity of the land of the nations is rabbinic, the halakha follows the lenient views. All the more so there is no room to be stringent within the borders of the State of Israel, since the basis of the prohibition is leaving the boundary of settlement, and the entire territory of the State of Israel is considered today the boundary of settlement, as explained below in halakha 17.
From the parameters of the prohibition on kohanim to leave the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia, we learn for all of Israel the parameters of the prohibition of leaving for outside the Land, and that it is permitted to leave for a great need, such as: livelihood, marrying a wife and studying Torah, as explained in Rambam (Hilkhot Melakhim 5:9). Some say that even for a short time it is forbidden to leave without a great need, just as kohanim were forbidden to leave without a great need even for a short time. However, in my humble opinion, kohanim were forbidden to leave for a short time because they immediately became impure, but for the rest of Israel the prohibition of leaving for outside the Land concerns a long time, and it was permitted only for a great need. When the departure is for a short time, such as less than a month, it is permitted to leave for any need, since this is a very temporary departure and does not harm the permanence of dwelling in the Land. Except that one who leaves loses during those days the mitzva of being in the Land of Israel; however, this mitzva is optional and not obligatory (Peninei Halakha: Likkutim, The Nation and the Land 3:9).

sections.body_en:
The mitzva of ḥalla applies in the Land of Israel when the majority of Israel is in the Land, as it is stated (Bamidbar 15:18-19): "When you come into the land to which I bring you, then it shall be, when you eat of the bread of the land, that you shall set apart a teruma (gift) to the Lord." The Sages learned (Ketubot 25a): "'When you come' – I spoke of the coming of all of you, and not the coming of some of you." Therefore, when Israel came up to the Land in the days of Ezra, they were not obligated in the mitzva, since only some of them came up to the Land. However, the Men of the Great Assembly, headed by Ezra the Scribe, instituted that even when the majority of Israel is not in the Land, ḥalla is to be separated (Rambam, Hilkhot Bikkurim 5:5).

Not only that, but the Sages further instituted that ḥalla be separated throughout the world as well, so that the laws of ḥalla would not be forgotten from Israel (Bekhorot 27a; Rambam, ibid. 5:7). They instituted this for ḥalla and not for terumot and ma'asrot because the mitzva of ḥalla is similar to the mitzvot that depend on the person and not on the soil, since one becomes obligated in it at the time of kneading (Tosafot, Kiddushin 36b). Moreover, the mitzva of ḥalla pertains to everyone, whereas the mitzva of terumot and ma'asrot pertains only to farmers (Mahari Kurkus, Hilkhot Bikkurim 5:7).

After the Sages decreed impurity on the land of the nations, that is, on all the territories outside the boundary of settlement of those who came up from Babylonia, it was no longer possible to eat the ḥalla in all the impure places, since the ḥalla is holy and must be eaten in purity. Therefore the Sages instituted that in the Land of Israel within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt two ḥallot be separated: one ḥalla of the measure the Sages fixed, one forty-eighth, and this is to be burned since it is impure, and through this people will remember that the ḥalla is holy and it is forbidden to eat it in impurity. And another ḥalla is to be separated, of whatever amount the owner of the dough wishes, even a minimal amount, and this is to be given to a kohen, so that people will remember the purpose of the ḥalla, which is meant to be eaten by the kohanim. The kohanim may eat it in impurity, provided they are not impure with an impurity that issues from the body, such as a seminal emission or nidda; and if they became impure through these, after they immerse for their purification they may eat this ḥalla.

In Syria and in all the other lands of the world, where the basis of the obligation of ḥalla is at a lower level, the law is different. When there is a kohen there who is not impure with an impurity that issues from his body, such as a minor who has not yet become impure at all, or an adult who has immersed, one ḥalla is separated and he eats it. When there is no kohen there who is pure of impurity that issues from his body, two ḥallot are separated: one is to be burned, so as to remember that it is forbidden to eat ḥalla in impurity, and for this ḥalla one may separate even a minimal amount. The second may be eaten even by kohanim who are impure with impurity that issues from the body, and its measure is one forty-eighth (Mishna Ḥalla 4:8; Bekhorot 27a; Rambam, Hilkhot Bikkurim 5:7-11).12

Since purity ceased from Israel, kohanim cannot eat ḥalla in the Land of Israel, and therefore in the Land one ḥalla of a minimal amount is separated, and the ḥalla is burned. Some say that this is the practice outside the Land as well, since the basis of the enactment to separate two ḥallot outside the Land was so that people would remember the mitzva of eating the ḥalla that the kohanim eat in the Land; and when ḥalla is not eaten in the Land, outside the Land too there is no room to separate an additional ḥalla for eating, but only one ḥalla for burning, as in the Land of Israel. And this is the prevalent custom (above, 11:4, note 2).

notes_en.en:
In the places on which impurity was decreed, they instituted that two ḥallot be separated, so that people would remember on the one hand that it is forbidden to eat ḥalla in impurity, and therefore the first is burned, and so that they would remember that the ḥalla is meant to be eaten by kohanim, and therefore the second ḥalla is eaten. In the boundary of those who came up from Egypt, which became obligated in ḥalla by Torah law in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun, the law that it is forbidden to eat ḥalla in impurity is more prominent, and therefore the ḥalla that is burned is the main one, and it must be of the measure that the Sages fixed – though the lower measure that they fixed, one forty-eighth (above, 11:2) – and the ḥalla that is eaten, which is not the main one, has no fixed measure. And in Syria and outside the Land, where the basis of ḥalla is rabbinic, the main point of the enactment was to separate an additional ḥalla to be eaten by the kohanim, and therefore the ḥalla that is burned has no fixed measure, while for the ḥalla that is eaten one must separate one forty-eighth (Mishna Ḥalla 4:8, and the commentators there). Regarding teruma, they did not institute separating two terumot, because this involves halakhic complications (since the additional teruma itself would become tevel from which ma'asrot had not been separated); therefore, from the time they decreed impurity on the earth of the land of the nations, only a kohen pure of impurity that issues from his body was permitted to eat teruma outside the Land (Bekhorot 27a; Yerushalmi Ḥalla 4:4).
What I wrote above regarding Syria and outside the Land follows the view of Rambam that there are three levels of places with respect to the law of ḥalla. However, according to Tosafot (Bekhorot 27a, s.v. "hilkhakh") and the Rosh, all that is explained above concerns Babylonia and the other lands far from the Land of Israel, where, when there is a kohen pure of impurity that issues from his body, only one ḥalla is separated. But in Syria and the adjacent lands, such as Amon and Moav, even when there is a kohen pure of impurity from his body, two ḥallot are separated: one of a minimal amount, which is burned, and the second of the fixed measure, which is eaten by any kohen, even one impure with impurity that issues from his body.
Unlike the law of terumot and ma'asrot, where according to many Rishonim the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot is by Torah law even when a minority of Israel is in the Land, regarding ḥalla nearly all the Rishonim hold that at a time when the majority of Israel is not in the Land the obligation of ḥalla is rabbinic; and so wrote Rambam (Hilkhot Bikkurim 5:5) and SA YD 322:2. However, regarding ḥalla too, some hold that when the Land was sanctified a second time in the days of Ezra, the obligation of ḥalla took effect by Torah law, even though only a minority of Israel was in the Land, and this obligation continues forever (a view brought in Tashbetz 2:291 and in Levush 322:2).

sections.title_en: Terumot and Ma'asrot: By Torah Law or by Rabbinic Law
sections.body_en:
It is agreed that the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land a second time, so that Israel would again become obligated in fulfilling the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land, including terumot and ma'asrot.

However, the Amora'im and the Rishonim disagreed whether through this we became obligated in terumot and ma'asrot by Torah law or by rabbinic law. According to many Rishonim, from the time the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land, they became obligated in the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot by Torah law. And regarding the period after the Temple was destroyed they disagreed: some say that the obligation still remains in place, because the Land was sanctified forever (Rashi, Ra'avad and Kaftor Va-feraḥ). And some say that after the Temple was destroyed, the obligation became rabbinic (Rashba, Ritva, Ran and Sefer Ha-teruma).

According to Rambam, even after the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land, the obligation of the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot was rabbinic, because the obligation of the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot, like the mitzva of ḥalla, applies by Torah law only when the majority of Israel dwells in its Land. Nevertheless, the sanctity with which the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land was effective with regard to the very obligation to fulfil the mitzva. And this obligation determines that when the majority of Israel is not in the Land, the obligation is rabbinic, and when the majority of Israel dwells in the Land, they will be obligated by Torah law without any need to sanctify the Land again. And so the later poskim wrote, that the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot in our time is rabbinic, and when the majority of Israel is in the Land, the obligation will be by Torah law.13

notes_en.en: The ruling in SA and Rema (331:2) follows the view of Rambam. And so wrote Radbaz 2:731; Mabit 2:196; Maharit 1:25; Levush 331:2; the Gra 331:6, and many others. And so wrote Mishpetei Eretz 3:1; Gevulot Ha-sadeh 3:15. See above, note 8, regarding the disagreement about the second sanctity, and there it was explained that the main view is that the Land was sanctified forever by Torah law for all the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land, except that in practice the obligation of shevi'it is rabbinic, because its Torah obligation depends on Israel dwelling on their land in the proper manner, each tribe in its inheritance. And the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot is rabbinic because, according to Rambam, its Torah obligation applies only when the majority of its inhabitants are upon it. And so wrote the Maggid Mishneh (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 20:3) and Beit Yosef (331:1). However, we have learned that according to the Gra (331:6, based on Rambam), their sanctification was rabbinic from the outset, but we have already learned in Rambam (Hilkhot Terumot 1:26) that in the third possession, when the majority of its inhabitants are upon it, we will be obligated by Torah law without an additional sanctification (see Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 11:3-4).

sections.title_en: The Other Places with Respect to Terumot and Ma'asrot
sections.body_en:
As we have learned (in halakha 8), when the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land, they sanctified the area of settlement, that is, the area of "those who came up from Babylonia," and through this the sanctity was reawakened also in all the places that those who came up from Egypt had conquered on both sides of the Jordan, and it even spread to Syria. And the Sages determined that by force of that sanctity all the places would be obligated to fulfil the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land, except that within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia the foundation of the obligation of the mitzvot is by Torah law, and within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and in Syria it is by rabbinic law. In later times Yoḥanan the High Priest instituted the enactment of "demai," according to which one must separate, out of doubt, ma'asrot and terumat ma'aser from produce bought from amei ha-aretz (people not reliable regarding tithes), and he determined that this enactment would apply to the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia and not to the boundary of those who came up from Egypt. This is the only difference in the law of terumot and ma'asrot between the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia and the boundary of those who came up from Egypt according to most Rishonim, and so the Aḥaronim ruled.

However, some Rishonim hold that the difference between them is greater: that within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia one must separate terumot and ma'asrot from all fruits and vegetables, according to the enactment of the Sages, whereas within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt one must separate only from grain, wine and oil, whose obligation is by Torah law (Rashi, Ra'avad and Kaftor Va-feraḥ).14

In Syria it is agreed that by the basic law one must separate terumot and ma'asrot, but many were accustomed not to separate, because they held that even lands bought by Jews actually belonged to the king, and land of a gentile in Syria is exempt from terumot and ma'asrot even when a Jew completed the work of gathering the produce (Gittin 47a; above, end of note 4). However, in practice the poskim wrote that one must separate terumot and ma'asrot in Syria from land registered in the name of a Jew.15

notes_en.en:
We have learned in the Mishna (Demai 1:3): "From Keziv onward is exempt from demai." From Keziv onward is the boundary of those who came up from Egypt; thus, regarding demai they are exempt, and regarding tevel they are obligated. And what we learned (Ḥullin 6b), that Rabbi Meir ate a vegetable in Beit She'an without tithing it, and on the basis of this Rabbi Yehuda Ha-nasi exempted Beit She'an – the meaning is that he ate a demai vegetable, and we learn that even though Beit She'an was within the area of those who came up from Babylonia, since it was a mostly gentile city, they refrained from taking hold of it and sanctifying it, and left it at the level of the boundary of those who came up from Egypt. So wrote Rabbeinu Tam, Ramban, Rashba, Ritva and Tosafot Ha-Rosh. And Rambam agrees with the principle that within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt one must separate terumot and ma'asrot from all produce and is exempt only from demai, except that in his view the gentile cities were exempted entirely from terumot and ma'asrot, even though they have the status of the boundary of those who came up from Egypt. And such was the law of Ashkelon, Caesarea and Beit She'an (Hilkhot Terumot 1:5).
And some hold that the difference is deeper: that within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia one must separate terumot and ma'asrot from all produce, whereas within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt one must separate only from grain, wine and oil, for we have already learned (above, 8:1) that according to most Rishonim only these species are obligated in terumot and ma'asrot by Torah law. And this is what Rabbi [Yehuda Ha-nasi] determined on the basis of the incident with Rabbi Meir: that the law of Beit She'an is like the law of the boundary of those who came up from Egypt, and there is no need to separate terumot and ma'asrot from vegetables there (Rashi, Ra'avad and Kaftor Va-feraḥ). And a few individuals hold that within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and the gentile cities they were entirely exempt from the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot (Rabbeinu Gershom and Tashbetz). In halakha, the Aḥaronim agree that one must separate terumot and ma'asrot from all kinds of produce even within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and in Syria, and they were exempted only from the enactment of demai (Sha'arei Tzedek 13:44; Gevulot Ha-sadeh 3:8). Regarding the gentile cities, one could rely on Rambam and not separate terumot and ma'asrot there, but since there is doubt about the exact area of the exemption, and according to most Rishonim they are obligated in terumot and ma'asrot, the ruling is to separate terumot and ma'asrot there without a blessing (see Mishpetei Eretz 3:6). Today, after the establishment of the State of Israel, in all the places under its rule one is obligated in terumot and ma'asrot fully and with a blessing (as explained below in note 20).

In Syria many were accustomed not to separate terumot and ma'asrot, but the God-fearing would separate. Rav Laniado, the rabbi of Aram Tzova (Aleppo), wrote (Beit Dino Shel Shlomo 3) that they were accustomed to be lenient on the claim that the kingdom has a right in the land, and the taxes the farmers pay are like rent, and since in Syria the halakha is that a gentile's ownership cancels the mitzva, terumot and ma'asrot are not separated. But he himself did not accept this reasoning, and ruled that terumot and ma'asrot be separated from land in the hands of Jews. And so is the view of many, among them: Maharam Galante (no. 57), the rabbi of Damascus, in Nivḥar Mi-kesef (YD 23), and the Ḥida (Shiyurei Berakha 331:1). Even so, some recorded the custom of not separating as halakha (Mishpetei Eretz 3:9). Regarding ma'aser sheni in Syria, see above at the end of note 4.

sections.title_en: Terumot and Ma'asrot Outside the Land
sections.body_en:
As we have learned (in halakha 5), the prophets and the Sages instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated in four lands adjacent to the Land: Babylonia, Egypt, Amon and Moav. And even after the Sages decreed impurity on the land of the nations, the Sages determined that the kohanim may eat the terumot there, on condition that they are not impure with an impurity that issues from the body (above, 10). They were not permitted to bring the produce of "ma'aser sheni" up to Jerusalem; rather, they would redeem it for money in order to buy food with it in Jerusalem (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni 1:14). And since the mitzva of shemita does not apply outside the Land, they instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated in shevi'it as well.

In practice, already in the period of the Ge'onim it was not the custom to separate terumot and ma'asrot in the four lands adjacent to the Land, and the Ge'onim explained that since the practice of purity ceased in Israel, the enactment to separate terumot and ma'asrot outside the Land lapsed. Admittedly, in Rambam and the Shulḥan Arukh it is ruled that one must separate terumot and ma'asrot in those four lands, and some say that this is the proper practice ideally. However, in practice the custom is not to separate terumot and ma'asrot outside the Land at all.16

notes_en.en: Rambam (Hilkhot Terumot 1:1, 4) and SA (331:1) wrote straightforwardly that one must separate terumot and ma'asrot in Babylonia, Egypt, Amon and Moav. However, in practice, already in the period of the Ge'onim the custom was not to separate terumot and ma'asrot there, and Rav Tzemaḥ Gaon explained (Teshuvot Ha-Ge'onim, Beitza 12b) that the enactment was observed as long as they were careful about the laws of impurity and purity and the kohanim would eat their teruma. That is, although they were impure with the impurity of the land of the nations, they guarded themselves against other impurities. But from the time they stopped being careful about this, they also stopped separating terumot and ma'asrot. His words are cited in the Meiri, Nidda 32a; Kaftor Va-feraḥ 15; Mahari Kurkus, Hilkhot Bikkurim 5:7. Similarly wrote the Ittur and the Mikhtam. And so the Radbaz testified in his Responsa (2:659) that the custom in Egypt was not to separate terumot and ma'asrot, and so it is brought in Kisei Eliyahu (331:1) and Nehar Mitzrayim (Hilkhot Ḥalla 6). However, since Rambam (Hilkhot Terumot 1:1) and SA (331:1) wrote straightforwardly that terumot and ma'asrot are separated there, Ḥazon Ovadia (Terumot 1) wrote that this is the proper practice. (Gevulot Ha-sadeh 3, note 9, even wrote that one may recite a blessing over it.) However, the clear custom is that terumot and ma'asrot are not separated there, as written by Rav Tikochinsky (Eretz Yisrael 2, 8:7), Mishpetei Eretz (3:10) and Kedushat Ha-aretz (1:28).

sections.body_en:
Nearly all the Tanna'im agree that about a hundred and fifty years before the destruction of the First Temple, when the king of Assyria exiled the members of the tribes of Re'uven, Gad and half of Menashe, the Torah obligation of the mitzvot of shevi'it and yovel lapsed. For only when Israel dwells in its Land in the proper manner, the majority of each tribe in its inheritance, is one obligated in the mitzvot of shevi'it and yovel by Torah law (Arakhin 32b; Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 5:4, note 3). It follows, then, that the sanctity with which the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land with respect to the mitzvot of shevi'it and yovel established that although in the days of the Second Temple they were not obligated to fulfil them by Torah law, they would be obligated to fulfil them by rabbinic enactment. Furthermore, the sanctity with which they sanctified the Land is effective for the time when Israel returns to its Land, each tribe to its inheritance, so that the obligation of shevi'it and yovel will again apply by Torah law without any need to sanctify the Land again.

Even after the destruction of the Second Temple, the rabbinic obligation to observe shevi'it did not lapse. Admittedly, a doubt arose as to when the seventh year is, and in addition some Rishonim hold that from the time the beit din that sanctified months and counted years ceased from Israel, about three hundred years after the destruction of the Second Temple, the obligation to rest in shevi'it lapsed, and it is good to observe shevi'it in our time only as a custom of piety (Razah and Ra'avad). However, in practice the view of the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim is that even today one must observe shevi'it by rabbinic law, according to the count accepted among us (Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 5:6-7, notes 5-6).
