In the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and in Syria too, one is obligated to rest in shevi'it, except that within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia the Sages decreed not to eat sefiḥim, that is, vegetables that grow by themselves, whereas within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and in Syria they did not decree this (Rambam, Semag, Ḥinukh and others). Some are lenient and hold that within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and in Syria it is even permitted to eat the produce of shevi'it after the time of bi'ur (removal). And some say that their produce does not even have sanctity.17

notes_en.en: The view of the overwhelming majority of the poskim is that the prohibition of working the land in shevi'it applies also to the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and to Syria, and the entire distinction between the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia and the rest of the Land is in the prohibition of sefiḥim alone (Rambam, Semag, Ḥinukh, Kaftor Va-feraḥ, Tiferet Yisrael, Nivḥar Mi-kesef, Ma'amar Mordekhai and Mishpetei Eretz, and many others). Some say that there is also no law of bi'ur for the produce that grows there (Rash and Ramban), and some say that there is also no law of shevi'it sanctity for the produce that grows there (Maharit, the Gra and Pe'at Ha-shulḥan). Admittedly, a few Rishonim hold that there is no prohibition of working the land outside the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia. So wrote Rabbeinu Gershom, Rashi, the Meiri (Ḥullin 6b) and Tashbetz (3:199). However, all the other poskim did not accept their words, and therefore I did not cite them in Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 5:8, note 7.

sections.body_en:
The mitzvot of leket, shikheḥa, pe'a, peret and olelot, which are left for the poor in the fields, apply by Torah law in the Land of Israel only. And just as they instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated in the lands close to the Land of Israel, so they instituted regarding the gifts for the poor throughout the lands outside the Land (Rambam; Tur 332:1), and some say that they instituted this only for the lands adjacent to the Land (Ha-ittur; Shakh, 2).

Although the enactment of giving terumot and ma'asrot outside the Land lapsed in the period of the Ge'onim, the enactment of the gifts for the poor did not lapse. This is because the terumot and "ma'aser sheni" depend on the observance of purity and the Temple service, and therefore we fulfil them in the Land of Israel after the destruction only because of the obligation of the mitzva, without their serving the purposes for which they were established; but outside the Land there is no reason to continue the enactment when it serves no purpose. The gifts for the poor, however, were of benefit to the Jewish poor outside the Land as well, and therefore even after the destruction of the Temple the enactment to leave them the gifts remained in place. However, today it is not the custom to leave gifts for the poor, since it is not worthwhile for the poor to take them (as explained above, 6:9).

The poskim disagreed regarding the force of the obligation of the gifts for the poor in the Land of Israel in our time. Their disagreement depends on the question of whether this mitzva is considered an individual mitzva or a communal one, as explained above (halakha 4, and end of note 2). Some say that the mitzva is rabbinic only (Ḥinukh 216; Pe'at Ha-shulḥan 4:39). And some say it is by Torah law (Minḥat Ḥinukh 216:15; Degel Re'uven, part 2, 28-29), and the Torah obligation applies throughout the boundary of those who came up from Egypt (Yeshu'ot Malko, Terumot 1:26).

Reshit ha-gez (the first shearing): The Tanna'im disagreed on the question of whether the mitzva of reshit ha-gez applies outside the Land as well, and the halakha was ruled that it does not apply outside the Land, just as terumot and ma'asrot do not apply outside the Land (Ḥullin 136b; SA YD 333:1). Regarding the force of the mitzva of "reshit ha-gez" in the Land of Israel, some say that it is by Torah law, and some say that its obligation is rabbinic, like the law of terumot and ma'asrot.18

The foreleg, the cheeks and the maw: According to all the poskim, in all the territories under the rule of the State of Israel one is obligated by Torah law to give them.

However, regarding the obligation of the mitzva outside the Land they disagreed. According to many poskim the mitzva of giving them is equivalent to the mitzvot of reshit ha-gez and terumot and ma'asrot, and consequently one is not obligated to separate them outside the Land (Rashi, Tosafot, Ha-ma'or, Rashba). And some say that only from the mitzva of reshit ha-gez, which was equated with terumot and ma'asrot, is one exempt outside the Land, but in the other gifts from animals one is obligated, since the animal does not grow from the ground, and all the mitzvot pertaining to it apply outside the Land as well (Rambam, Hilkhot Bikkurim 9:1). In practice, the custom outside the Land is not to give the gifts to a kohen (SA 61:21), and some who are meticulous have been accustomed to give them.19

notes_en.en: As we learned in halakha 11, according to Rashi, Ra'avad and Kaftor Va-feraḥ, the law of terumot and ma'asrot is by Torah law even after the destruction, since the second sanctity did not lapse. And according to Rashba, Ritva, Ran and Sefer Ha-teruma, the second sanctity lapsed with the destruction and the law of terumot and ma'asrot became rabbinic. However, below in note 20 it is explained that according to their view, after the establishment of the State, the sanctity returned to obligate the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot by Torah law. And according to Rambam and the Ḥinukh, although the foundation of the second sanctity is by Torah law even during the period of destruction, the law of terumot and ma'asrot depends on the majority of Israel being in the Land, and this is agreed in practice by the Aḥaronim. But they disagreed regarding "reshit ha-gez": according to Rambam its obligation is rabbinic, like the law of teruma (Mahari Kurkus, Hilkhot Bikkurim 10:1; Pri Megadim; Minḥat Ḥinukh 506). And from the Ḥinukh it is implied that its obligation is by Torah law, since reshit ha-gez was not equated with teruma in every respect, but only with respect to the exemption from the mitzva outside the Land (Minḥat Ḥinukh 508).

As we learned regarding "reshit ha-gez," according to all who hold that its law depends on the sanctity of the Land, its obligation within the area of the State of Israel is by Torah law. Only according to Rambam is the mitzva of reshit ha-gez rabbinic in the Land, since it was equated with the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot, whose Torah obligation depends on the majority of Israel. However, according to Rambam himself the mitzva of the foreleg, the cheeks and the maw obligates by Torah law throughout the world and at all times; it follows that according to all views the mitzva of the foreleg, the cheeks and the maw in the Land is by Torah law.

sections.body_en:
The status of all the territories under the control of the State of Israel is like the status of the area of those who came up from Babylonia, in which the foundation of the obligation of all the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land applies by Torah law. And also the territories within the area of those who came up from Egypt, the foundation of whose obligation in the days of the Second Temple was rabbinic – if they are under Israeli control, the foundation of their obligation is by Torah law, like the law of the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia. For we have learned that the second sanctity, with which the Land was sanctified in the days of Ezra, sanctified the Land for all generations, as it is stated (Devarim 30:5): "And the Lord your God will bring you into the land which your fathers possessed, and you shall possess it …" The Sages said: they have a first and a second possession, but not a third. That is, they would need to sanctify the Land the first time in the days of Yehoshua, and the second time in the days of Ezra, but not a third time. From this they learned that even after the destruction of the Second Temple, the sanctity of the Land for its mitzvot did not lapse (Yevamot 82b; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 1:5; above, 7). And although at the time of the Second Temple only the area in which those who came up from Babylonia settled was sanctified by Torah law, since we have learned that there is no further third sanctity, it follows that when the boundary of Jewish settlement expands, the sanctity too expands with it. Just as it was at the time of the Second Temple, when at first only the area around Jerusalem was sanctified, since only there was there Jewish settlement, and as the settlement expanded the sanctity too spread with it. And even after the destruction of the Temple, the sanctity did not depart from the boundary of settlement of those who came up from Babylonia. So too in our days, the sanctity that determines the obligation of the mitzvot dependent on the Land applies to all the places under Israeli rule.

And even according to those who hold that the second sanctity lapsed with the destruction of the Second Temple, the sovereignty of the State of Israel, in the name of the people of Israel as a whole, over the territories of the Land of Israel brings upon them the sanctity that determines the Torah obligation of the mitzvot. As Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Terumot 1:2): "The Land of Israel mentioned everywhere refers to the lands that a king of Israel, or a judge, or a prophet conquers with the consent of the majority of Israel, and this is what is called a conquest of the many." And he further wrote (Hilkhot Melakhim 5:6): "All the lands that Israel conquers with a king by authority of the beit din – this is a conquest of the many, and it is like the Land of Israel that Yehoshua conquered in every respect." And our master Rav Kook ztz"l ruled (Mishpat Kohen 144) that when there is no king, the authority of the king passes to the nation as a whole, and whatever is done in the name of the people of Israel has full force. And the Jews who live in the Land are the ones who represent the nation (Horayot 3a).20

Therefore, all the territories under the rule of the State of Israel are obligated in terumot and ma'asrot with a blessing, and one may separate terumot and ma'asrot from produce grown in one place for produce grown in another place. However, it is not proper to separate from produce grown in territories under the rule of other states for produce grown in the State of Israel, or vice versa, because some hold that in the territories under Israeli rule the foundation of the mitzva is by Torah law, and in the territories outside the borders of the State the foundation of the mitzva is rabbinic.

When the majority of Israel dwells in the Land, according to all views the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot will be by Torah law in all the territories under Israeli rule (see Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 11:3-4, on the number of Jews in the world).21

notes_en.en:
According to Rambam (Hilkhot Terumot 1:5; Hilkhot Beit Ha-beḥira 6:16), and so it is agreed by the later poskim, the second sanctity sanctified for its time and for the future, and therefore there will be no further need to sanctify the Land of Israel with a third sanctity. Accordingly, when Israel conquers territories in the Land throughout its expanses up to the river Euphrates and settles in them, the Torah obligation extends to them. For since there will be no third sanctity, the same sanctity with which the area of those who came up from Babylonia was sanctified spreads to all the territories under the control of the people of Israel. (However, for an incidental reason – that the majority of its inhabitants are not upon it – terumot and ma'asrot and shevi'it apply today by rabbinic law, as explained above in halakhot 11 and 14.)
Some Rishonim hold that the second sanctity lapsed, and that the Land will be sanctified a third time (Rashba, Ran, Ritva, Sefer Ha-teruma, as cited above in halakha 7, halakha 11, and note 8). Even according to their view, the Land is sanctified through settlement, and all the more so through settlement and sovereignty. And so it is written in the Hilkhot Eretz Yisrael 9-10 attributed to the Tur: "In my opinion, sanctification of the place is not required for any of what those who came up from Egypt conquered, and even today, if there is one city in the Land of Israel designated for the dwelling of Jews, and the fields are designated for Jews, and there is no fear of a gentile who could expel them from it – this is its sanctity, and it is obligated in tithes by Torah law." And so wrote the Maharit (1:25), that even for the second sanctity no verbal sanctification was needed; rather, the sanctification took place through the settlement. And according to the Radbaz (Hilkhot Terumot 1:5), the first sanctity was effected through conquest, and in the second, where there was no conquest, it was necessary to sanctify verbally through Ezra and his beit din. If so, today, when we have conquered the Land, there is no need for verbal sanctification.
Some raise a difficulty from what we learned in Rambam (Hilkhot Melakhim 5:6), that the king must conquer the Land by authority of the beit din (implying that the intent is the Great Beit Din, whose judges are ordained), and the IDF did not conquer by authority of the beit din. However, the need for a beit din is only in order to decide on going out to an optional war, to conquer territories when there is no necessity. But when Israel is attacked, according to all views there is a Torah mitzva to go out to a defensive war (Rambam, ibid. 1), and whatever is conquered in this war is done within the framework of an obligatory war. And so wrote Rav Goren (Torat Ha-mo'adim, p. 658). And although the majority of Israel is not in the Land, we have learned in Horayot (3a) that those who dwell in the Land are considered the people of Israel as a whole, and consequently what they conquer becomes sanctified. And so wrote Rav Goren there. Moreover, since the conquest by the IDF was carried out on behalf of the people of Israel as a whole, as all the Jews of the world are entitled to immigrate to the Land, it was carried out in the name of the people of Israel as a whole. Furthermore, the Mabit wrote (Kiryat Sefer, Terumot 1) regarding the boundary of those who came up from Egypt, that the majority of Israel is not needed in order to sanctify it again.
Regarding Eilat an additional discussion arose, because according to most views it is outside the boundary of those who came up from Egypt, since it is south of the border of Parashat Mas'ei; and then some hold that Israeli rule does not serve to sanctify it, because although it is within the broad borders of the Land (Peninei Halakha: Likkutim, The Nation and the Land 3:14), it cannot be sanctified before the conquest of the borders of Parashat Mas'ei is completed (Eretz Ḥemda, part 1, Sha'ar 3, 6:3; 13:2; and Ohala Shel Torah, part 3, 1:4, inclined to this. And so it is implied from the position of rabbis of the Ḥaredi circles, as Rav Kalman Kahana wrote at the end of "Ha-shevi'it Tishmetena"). However, many wrote that sovereignty over Eilat is effective, and so it seems for several reasons: a) Because the Sages said that David acted improperly in initiating the conquest of Syria before the Temple Mount, but in our days, all the wars began as defence and all the conquests were made for the sake of security and deterrence, and therefore they were done properly. b) After Jerusalem was sanctified with the first sanctity forever, and the Land was sanctified with the second sanctity forever (according to Rambam and all the Aḥaronim), there is no longer a need to follow the order, and every place that is conquered becomes sanctified (Rav Goren).
c) Some say that only the Canaanite nations had to be conquered first, but today, when their memory has been lost, there is no need first to conquer their place (She'ilat David, Kuntres Ha-ḥiddushim be-Inyenei Shevi'it). d) Some hold that in fact the entire Negev up to Eilat is within the area of those who came up from Egypt, since the kingdom of Shlomo extended up to there, and perhaps it was even within the border of Parashat Mas'ei, since some hold that "Ma'ale Akrabim" is Akaba, which is adjacent to Eilat (Rasag, Rav Tikochinsky and Rav Eliyahu). And some say that the boundary of those who came up from Egypt extends over the entire Land of Israel, from the River of Egypt to the river Euphrates, and Eilat is included in this (Rav Yisrael Ariel, Otzar Eretz Yisrael 5:30). On the basis of these reasons and additional ones, the law of the territories under Israeli sovereignty up to Eilat is like the law of the "boundary of those who came up from Babylonia." And so many wrote in practice, among them: Rav Goren (Torat Ha-mo'adim, p. 658; "Emunat Itekha" 50); Tzitz Eliezer 10:1; Rav Gershuni (Or Ha-mizraḥ 22); Rav Aryeh Stern ("Emunat Itekha" 50); Rav Wittman (Shemita Mamlakhtit, chapter 11, 6); Rav Zoldan ("Malkhut Yehuda Ve-Yisrael," no. 24); Rav Neḥemya Rata (Or Ha-ner 2).

In principle, the foundation of the obligation in the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia is by Torah law, and within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt it is rabbinic (above, halakha 8). However, regarding the level of the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot in our time, three views were stated: a) In the days of the Second Temple, within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia they were obligated in terumot and ma'asrot by Torah law, and after the Temple was destroyed the obligation became rabbinic (Rashba, Ran, Ritva and Sefer Ha-teruma). And according to what we learned in the previous note, according to this view the obligation today in all the places under Israeli rule is by Torah law. b) Even after the destruction of the Temple, the obligation within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia remained by Torah law (Rashi, Ra'avad and Kaftor Va-feraḥ). And according to this view too, the Torah obligation today extends to all the territories under Israeli rule. c) According to Rambam (Hilkhot Terumot 1:5, 26), although the foundation of the obligation within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia is by Torah law, as long as the majority of Israel is not in the Land, the obligation in practice is rabbinic. And this is the view accepted in halakha (above, halakha 11).
Thus, until the establishment of the State, only according to the second view was the obligation within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia by Torah law, and within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt rabbinic; but according to the first view, and likewise according to the third view, which was accepted in halakha, before the establishment of the State the obligation in all the territories was rabbinic, and consequently one could separate from the produce of one for the other. Admittedly, some were in doubt, according to the view accepted in halakha, whether perhaps ideally one should not separate from the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia, whose obligation according to Rambam rests on one rabbinic factor (that the majority of its inhabitants are not upon it), for the boundary of those who came up from Egypt, whose obligation rests on two rabbinic factors (since it was also not sanctified in the days of Ezra) (Malbushei Yom Tov, Ḥovat Ha-karka, no. 17. Rav Tikochinsky, in Hilkhot Eretz Yisrael, part 2, 8:4, was stringent, and Torat Ha-aretz 1:8 was lenient). And some say that with respect to the level of obligation in the Land, even two rabbinic factors are considered as one (Ḥazon Ish, Shevi'it 3:34:2). In any case, all agree that after the fact, if one separated from one for the other, he has fulfilled his obligation, as explained above, 9, note 3.
However, after the establishment of the State of Israel, terumot and ma'asrot must be separated with a blessing from all the places under its rule, including the places that were in the boundary of those who came up from Egypt, and also the cities that were in the hands of gentiles. As we learned in the previous note, the conquest of the Land by Israel brings upon it the Torah sanctity of the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land. Except that according to Rambam, and so it was ruled in halakha according to the Aḥaronim, terumot and ma'asrot are rabbinic since the majority of its inhabitants are not upon it.
Some insist on arguing that Israeli rule does not change the status of the territories (see Mishpetei Eretz 3:6-7). And although they are mistaken, in any case, as we have learned, even before the State of Israel was established, the view of most poskim in practice is that the force of the obligation in the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot is rabbinic and equal in all the territories within the boundaries of those who came up from Babylonia and those who came up from Egypt. Only with respect to demai is there a difference, in that it applies within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia and not within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt. And so wrote Rabbeinu Tam, Ramban, Rashba, Ritva and Tosafot Ha-Rosh. And this is also the view of Rambam, and only regarding the gentile cities is his view that the Sages exempted them entirely from terumot and ma'asrot. And although we generally rule according to Rambam, since there is some doubt about the exact location of the gentile cities, and according to most Rishonim one must separate terumot and ma'asrot from them, the custom was to separate terumot and ma'asrot from them without a blessing (as explained above, note 14). But today, after the establishment of the State, even those who insist on doubting the force of the obligation of all the places as being like the law of those who came up from Babylonia can at least follow the view of those who hold that the law of the gentile cities was always like that of those who came up from Egypt, and separate terumot and ma'asrot from them with a blessing. Only regarding the southern Arava, according to those who hold that it is outside the boundary of those who came up from Egypt, is there no obligation of terumot and ma'asrot. However, since we have already learned that some hold that even Eilat is within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt, even before the establishment of the State, if they separated from one for the other, after the fact they fulfilled their obligation, since a rabbinic doubt is resolved leniently. All the more so today, after the establishment of the State, when the law of Eilat has become like the rest of the Land, because the main halakhic view is that every place under Israeli rule is obligated in terumot and ma'asrot at the level of the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia, as explained in the previous note. It seems that the territories of Sinai that were under Israeli rule also became obligated in terumot and ma'asrot at the level of the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia, but after the withdrawal they returned to their former status. As it was in the Hasmonean kingdom (above, note 9), where in the territories that were conquered and not settled, the second sanctity did not remain after the second destruction. For the complete sanctity applies forever once the place has been sanctified through both parts of the mitzva – conquest and full settlement.
However, one should not separate terumot and ma'asrot from territories under the control of the State of Israel for territories under the control of the state of Jordan or of Egypt, since according to the view of the Rashba and those who agree with him (who hold that the second sanctity lapsed at the time of the second destruction and returned at the time of the establishment of the State, as mentioned at the beginning of the note), the foundation of the obligation in the State of Israel is by Torah law, and in Transjordan it is rabbinic. And if it concerns territories in Transjordan outside the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia, then even according to the view of the Ra'avad and those who agree with him (who hold that the second sanctity did not lapse), their obligation is rabbinic. However, after the fact, if they separated, they fulfilled their obligation, since according to Rambam and most poskim the obligation of all the territories of the Land is rabbinic (Mishpetei Eretz 3:8 was not concerned for the views of the Rashba and those who agree with him, and of the Ra'avad and those who agree with him, and permitted separating from Transjordan for the State of Israel).
